entries.title: Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
entries.summary: An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in Ukraine's Kyiv region.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2

September 20, 2026

An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in Ukraine's Kyiv region.

Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit.

Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop.

Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine."

"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X.

According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election

Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed.

This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election.

Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections."

Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported.

Three children killed in Kyiv region

In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said.

Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died.

The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a warehouse of drone and missile maker Fire Point was struck in the Kyiv region. It also hit a cargo vessel and a postal logistics center in the Odesa region, saying both were used for military shipments.

Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Ed Sheeran speaks on Gaza in concert after Macklemore controversy
entries.summary: Sheeran called the Hamas-led attack in Israel "horrific" and described the war in Gaza as "catastrophic and unjustifiable" during his first concert since the Macklemore controversy erupted.
entries.content:
United States of America

Ed Sheeran speaks on Gaza after Macklemore controversy

September 20, 2026

Sheeran called the Hamas-led attack in Israel "horrific" and described the war in Gaza as "catastrophic and unjustifiable" during his first concert since the Macklemore controversy erupted.

British pop star Ed Sheeran has addressed the Israel-Palestine conflict, following a row over Macklemore's removal as a supporting act on the tour after the US rapper made pro-Palestinian comments on stage.

Performing in Philadelphia on Saturday night, the first concert since the controversy erupted, Sheeran said the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, which killed around 1,200 people and saw dozens taken hostage, was "horrific."

He also described Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, which killed more than 70,000 people, as "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate."

Sheeran also condemned the "systemic injustice" in the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government is pushing to expand Jewish settlements, which the United Nations has called a "flagrant violation of international law."

"I don't want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.

"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," he said.

Sheeran's latest statement was a reversal from his earlier stance on Instagram, when he said that his concert audiences "do not expect a political forum."

How did the controversy occur?

The pop singer's tour faced controversy after rapper Macklemore was dropped as a supporting act after he said "Free Palestine" at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey in early September.

Sheeran has denied being responsible, saying venues had threatened to cancel shows if Macklemore remained on the tour.

Macklemore posted on Instagram that billionaire Robert Kraft had told Sheeran that the rapper would not be allowed to perform at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which he owns.

Several supporting acts subsequently withdrew in solidarity with Macklemore, including musician Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe, as well as Sheeran's backing band — leaving one of the best-selling musical artists of all time without an opening act.

Pro-Palestinian demonstrators protest outside concert venue

Dozens of pro-Palestinian protesters rallied peacefully outside Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field before Sheeran's concert, waving Palestinian flags and chanting "Free, free Palestine."

Among the demonstrators was 18-year-old Brandon Ateke, who accused Sheeran of "complicity" with Kraft and others in silencing Macklemore.

"I decided to not attend the concert and instead attend the protest to bring light to the genocide going on in Gaza today," Ateke told AFP news agency.

The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI), a pro-Palestinian group, has called for a boycott of Sheeran's world tour.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
entries.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.
entries.content:
Germany

In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners

September 20, 2026

A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.

Abdu, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Abdu is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.

"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to health care and German courses, for example, affect me directly."

Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.

Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's Sunday election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, it is holding a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Abdu is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.

Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Abdu decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.

Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.

Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens.

That happens to be another one of Abdu's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said.

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.

More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Abdu, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."

Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: India news: PM Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
entries.summary: PM Narendra Modi has told a climate conference that developed countries emit six times more CO2 than India. Meanwhile, an IIT Bombay professor has been accused of caste abuse. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions

Published September 19, 2026last updated September 20, 2026

PM Narendra Modi has told a climate conference that developed countries emit six times more CO2 than India. Meanwhile, an IIT Bombay professor has been accused of caste abuse. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian Prime Minister Modi tells a climate conference in Delhi that developing nations are unfairly blamed for emissions
  • IIT Bombay professor booked over alleged caste abuse after a student killed himself
  • Scottish-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without being convicted, has been granted bail
  • India had to replace Asian Games opening ceremony male flagbearer over missing ceremonial ⁠kit

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Saturday, September 19 and Sunday, September 20:

Skip next section IIT Bombay under fire over caste abuse allegations after student's death

IIT Bombay under fire over caste abuse allegations after student's death

Mumbai police have filed a case against an IIT Bombay professor after a 20-year-old second-year student, Sahil Wakode, was found dead in his hostel room late Thursday, following allegations from his family that he had faced months of caste-based harassment.

Police registered charges against Suryanarayan D. and unidentified others under India's abetment-to-suicide law and provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, local media reported.

Wakode's father, Ravindra Wakode, alleged in his complaint that his son had been subjected to sustained casteist remarks and mental harassment over roughly three months, and that the professor — who was invigilating an exam Wakode was attending on the day he died — used caste-based slurs against him.

The complaint also mentioned the institute's director. Similar complaints were shared by other students, according to The Wire. These allegations have not been independently established.

Meanwhile, IIT Bombay claimed Wakode was found using a mobile phone during the exam, but no disciplinary action was taken. Instead, he had been counseled and assured it would not affect his academic record before he returned to his hostel room.

Students at the scene allege that the professor was seen yelling at Wakode.

IIT Bombay said in a statement shared by local media that "the circumstances surrounding the death are being looked into by the appropriate authorities."

The case has drawn campus protests, with students at IIT Bombay demanding the resignation of both the director and the professor involved. It is reportedly the third student death by suicide at the institute this year, following earlier incidents in February and July.

Skip next section Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference

Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output.

Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal.

Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average."

"In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India."

He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule.

The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change."

The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

Hello, this is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from around India this weekend.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the inauguration of an international climate conference in New Delhi, saying that developing countries are being unfairly blamed for carbon emissions. 

Meanwhile, the Allahabad High Court has directed the Uttar Pradesh Police to ensure the protection of a same-sex couple living together.

Finally, a professor at IIT Bombay is facing allegations of caste abuse after a young student killed himself.

For this and more, follow our blog.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

Over 10 years after my last day as a Delhi University student, I will wrap up this Saturday's coverage of events with the 2026 DUSU elections.

But we will be back tomorrow, so follow DW for more!

Skip next section WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the race for recognition

WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the race for recognition

One of the world's most valuable rice varieties, basmati carries strong historic ties to the Punjab region, which spans both India and Pakistan.

Both claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.

But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the fight over basmati rice is far from over.

Watch for more:

Skip next section ABVP sweeps DUSU polls as student safety, identity dominate campaign

ABVP sweeps DUSU polls as student safety, identity dominate campaign

The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), affiliated with the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), won three of four central posts in this year's Delhi University Students' Union elections, with its candidate Yash Dabas coming in from behind to be elected president.

Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen made history by winning the vice-presidential seat, defeating candidates fielded by both ABVP and the National Students' Union of India (NSUI), the student wing of the Indian National Congress.

In a university facing an acute shortage of hostels, student housing and safety dominated this year's campaign. This came after the September 6 collapse of a paying-guest building in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, which killed seven students. 

High rents, non-functional hostels, and a lack of affordable lodging near campus were central issues in candidate platforms.

Declaring his win, Dabas stressed the issue as he addressed the media: "We all witnessed the accident that occurred in Satya Niketan; we do not want such an incident to happen to anyone in the future, and that will be our first priority — conducting safety audits for every college, hostel, and PG."

Shokeen, an NSUI rebel who ran independently, built his campaign partly around the tragedy, vowing not to wear footwear until affected students got justice.

The election also unfolded in the shadow of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led satirical protest movement that organized weeks of demonstrations at Delhi's Jantar Mantar earlier this year, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in national entrance exams. 

While the CJP was not involved in the DUSU race directly, the movement shaped how many voters approached the election.

"Students were talking about what or ganisations stand for, whether they agree with their politics and whether voting can give them a greater say in issues concerning students," one student told news agency PTI, adding that many felt they "should not simply vote because a particular organisation has always been influential on campus."

Skip next section More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee

More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee

US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients.

The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status. 

Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions. 

The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful.

The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%.

When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning.

Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia.

He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit."

Skip next section Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide

Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide

Surendra Koli, a key figure in India's notorious 2006 Nithari serial killings case who was acquitted of all charges last year, was found dead at a tea stall he operated in Haridwar.

Police are treating the case as a suspected suicide.

Residents discovered Koli's body inside the rented stall and alerted authorities, Haridwar City Deputy Superintendent of Police Shishupal Singh Negi told local media.

No suicide note was found and the body was sent for post-mortem examination as investigators look into the circumstances.

Koli first drew national attention in 2006, when he was a domestic worker at businessman Moninder Singh Pandher's home in Noida. The discovery of human remains, including children's, in a drain behind Pandher's house sparked a major investigation and nationwide outrage.

Koli was convicted and sentenced to death in multiple cases beginning in 2009. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both Koli and Pandher for lack of evidence.

Two key observations were made: Koli's confession was inadmissible, as it was extracted after a long, unauthorized interrogation in police custody without adequate legal safeguards, and the prosecution could not prove that the remains uncovered from the "open, public" drain were based solely on Koli's statements.

The decision was upheld by India's Supreme Court in late 2025.

Reports suggest he moved to the northern city of Haridwar after the acquittal. Police identified Koli through an Aadhaar card found on his body.

Skip next section India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up

India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up

A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.

Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.

Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.

"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.

The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."

The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.

Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.

A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.

Skip next section Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody

Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody

The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody.

The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail.

Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding.

He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017.

He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued.

Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary.

"Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture."

Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed.

What did the court say in its ruling?

In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon."

The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached.

Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported.

"I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from and about India this weekend.

We lead our coverage with the news that British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without conviction, has been granted bail.

A UN panel in 2022 recognized it as a case of arbitrary detention, putting the Indian government's human rights record under the microscope.

The Asian Games kick off in Japan on Saturday, but it's not all smooth sailing for the Indian delegation's preparations.

India has announced a last-minute change of its male flagbearer for the opening ceremony after star shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor's ceremonial kit reportedly went missing.

Finally, counting is underway in elections for the Delhi University Student Union, this time under the shadow of the Cockroach Janata Party protests and the collapse of a building in the student hub of Satya Niketan.

For the latest on these stories and more, follow our blog.

entries.title: Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
entries.summary: Oktoberfest 2026 is underway but it's not just beer on offer in Munich this year; revelers can also get themselves a flu jab before heading to the tents. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs

Published September 19, 2026last updated September 20, 2026

Oktoberfest 2026 is underway but it's not just beer on offer in Munich this year; revelers can also get themselves a flu jab before heading to the tents. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Polls have opened in key state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

    -follow live here
  • Germany's famous Oktoberfest is underway in Munich — with flu jabs on offer as well as beer
  • Annual anti-abortion marches have taken place in Berlin and Cologne
  • A port union has warned that German seaports are at significant risk of cyberattacks and sabotage

Here is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of September 19-20, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Burglar bags baked goods and ice cream in cafe raid

Burglar bags baked goods and ice cream in cafe raid

A burglar with an apparent penchant for sweet treats broke into a cafe and opted for cake and ice cream instead of cash, North Rhine-Westphalia police said. 

According to investigators, the burglary took place at 2:30 am (0030 GMT) on Saturday in the town of Bad Salzuflen.

"We still do not know whether he deliberately had his sights set on the sweet loot or whether he was seized by a bit of hunger during the crime," a police spokesman said.

Witnesses have been urged to come forward with information they might have that could result in the arrest of the sweet thief.

Skip next section German car makers losing ground – study

German car makers losing ground – study

Germany's automobile giants are continuing to lose ground internationally, according to a new study published on Sunday.

Data compiled by multinational services network EY, previously known as Ernst & Young, found that, while German car manufacturers are still turning over more than their international rivals and still posting a combined profit, the gap is narrowing.

According to the study, German giants BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen turned over a combined €284 billion in the first half of 2026 – around €1.5 billion more than the second-placed Japanese car industry.

But that figure is down 2.9% on last year and 7% lower than the record-high set in 2023.

Profits are also down, with the €13 billion made by the three German market leaders representing the second-lowest half-year profit since 2017.

US, Japanese, Chinese and South Korean manufacturers, on the other hand, all posted record turnovers for the period.

Skip next section O'piekst is!: German doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs

O'piekst is!: German doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs

Munich's annual Oktoberfest officially got underway on Saturday when the first beer keg was opened with the traditional cry of O'zapft is! ("It has been tapped!").

But another slogan is also being promoted in Bavaria this year: O'piekst is! ("It has been pricked!") — as doctors offer vaccine jabs against flu and Covid-19.

"With so many people coming together in such tight spaces in the beer tents, the risk of infection at Oktoberfest is higher," explained Christoph Spinner, head of infectiology at Munich's Rechts der Isar hospital.

Oktoberfest coincides with the start of the annual flu season, and Spinner warned that less than a third of people who are recommended a flu jab have actually had one.

Beatrix Zurek, a health expert from the city-led initiative München impft! ("Munich vaccinates!") said: "It's our job to go where people are. And that means: Oktoberfest."

Skip next section Welcome back

Welcome back

Guten Morgen! And welcome back to our coverage of Germany on Sunday, 20 September.

Voters in two more German states head to the polls today as elections take place in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and in the capital, the city-state of Berlin.

We will have all you need to know about those elections in a separate blog which we will be launching when polls open at 8 a.m. local time, so keep an eye out for that.

And for all your non-election Germany news – stay right here!

Skip next section This blog is now paused

This blog is now paused

We are pausing our coverage on Saturday, 19 September and will be back on Sunday, 20 September with more headlines from Germany.

Skip next section Anti-abortion protests held in Cologne, Berlin

Anti-abortion protests held in Cologne, Berlin

Protests against abortion and assisted suicide took to the streets of the German capital Berlin as well as the western city of Cologne on Saturday, in protest dubbed "March for Life."

Police said some 2,200 took part in Berlin, whereas no figures on the Cologne protests were immediately available. Catholic bishops were among those attending.

Meanwhile in both cities, pro-choice protests were also held.

Abortion in Germany is banned but women are allowed to carry out the measure if the first 12 weeks of the pregnancy have not yet concluded. They are however obligated to hold consultations first, and the abortion can only be held at least three days after such consultations.

Exceptions are naturally if the pregnancy poses a risk to the woman's health.

Skip next section WATCH: Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win

WATCH: Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win

Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and one of Germany’s most prominent Jewish community leaders, has voiced her alarm at the Alternative for Germany's (AfD) landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.

Speaking to DW, she warned that some Jews are once again considering leaving Germany, saying years of efforts to rebuild trust after the Holocaust are being undermined. Knobloch described the rise of the far-right party as a serious threat, urged mainstream politicians to confront extremism more forcefully and called for greater engagement with young people.

Her comments come amid renewed concerns about antisemitism, political polarization, and reported death threats against her.

Skip next section Far-right AfD holds final rally before Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election

Far-right AfD holds final rally before Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party held on Saturday its final rally in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the Sunday vote in the eastern state.

Ulrich Siegmund, the party's winner in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, addressed a rally of some 1,000 AfD supporters in Schwerin, according to police estimates.

He said that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won but without an absolute majority, was also possible in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The latest ZDF Politbarometer poll puts the AfD in the eastern state one percentage point behind the Social Democrats (SPD); at 36% and 37% respectively. Next is the Left Party (Die Linke) at 9%, then the CDU at 6% and the Greens at 5%.

The AfD rally was also attended by the party's candidate in the state, Leif-Erik Holm, who echoed previous remarks that the election "should serve as a signal that this government must finally go." Several other AfD leaders have repeated the same calls since the results of the Saxony-Anhalt state vote.

The far-right party's final rally of the campaign also saw some 350 counter-demonstrators, according to police. No incidents were reported.

Skip next section Merz schedules CDU meeting with all party leaders to discuss election results

Merz schedules CDU meeting with all party leaders to discuss election results

In an unusual measure, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will convene the Christian Democratic Union leadership on Sunday to discuss the results of the state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

Unlike in previous state elections, Merz has invited the entire party executive committee to a formal meeting at 5:00 p.m. (1500 GMT) at the CDU headquarters in Berlin. The committee includes some 25 members, either electees or representatives by virtue of their offices.

Due to attend are the eight influential CDU premiers who backed him ahead of the election.

Compounding pressure has befallen the conservative chancellor since the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month, which saw the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narrowly missing out on an absolute majority, while Merz's CDU secured half their previous result.

Polls for the upcoming votes are also grim, with the CDU threatened with the prospect of falling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.

In the capital Berlin, where CDU is currently in power, polls suggest the conservative party is in a neck-and-neck race with the socialist Left Party.

Skip next section Germany's Carsten Breuer to become NATO's Military Committee chairman

Germany's Carsten Breuer to become NATO's Military Committee chairman

Germany's highest ranking military officer, General Carsten Breuer, will be the next chairman of NATO's Military Committee, after being voted into the role on Saturday.

"The support of the chiefs of defense of our NATO allies means a great deal to me. The alliance faces major challenges - for our security and peace in Europe and beyond," Breuer, who is also Germany's chief of defense, told German news agency DPA.

The position is considered among NATO's most influential ones.

Breuer succeeds Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and will take over as of July 2027.

Breuer was competing for the position against Canada's Chief of Defense General Jennie Carignan. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to head the committee.

Skip next section Cologne opera house reopens after 14-year redo

Cologne opera house reopens after 14-year redo

Cologne's cultural complex, which includes the city's main opera house, theater and children's opera, has finally reopened after renovation works that extended for some 14 years.

"With the reopening of our theaters, we are giving the city back a central place of meeting, inspiration and artistic freedom that belongs to all people of Cologne," Mayor Torsten Burmester said.

The western German state's opera house dates back to 1957, with the theater coming shortly after in 1962.

Since 2012, renovations on the pair commenced with an original budget of €250 million (roughly $287 million) that has somehow multiplied nearly three fold as the years rolled on.

The final price tag on the refurbishments stood at around €800 million.

In the 14 years it took to get the job done, Cologne's opera and theater houses had to relocate to other venues.

Celebrations of the reopening include music, dance, as well as other hands-on activities. On Sunday evening, the opening ceremony will conclude with a concert at the opera house.

Skip next section Kremlin envoy offers economic cooperation to AfD

Kremlin envoy offers economic cooperation to AfD

A senior Kremlin envoy has offered Russian help with Germany's energy supply in cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been widely criticized for its perceived links with Moscow.

The remarks by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy for international economic cooperation, come as voters are set to go to the polls in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, with the AfD locked in a close race with the ruling Social Democrats (SPD).

"Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will thrive again when affordable, reliable Nord Stream gas returns through joint work with AfD," Dmitriev wrote on X, using the German name for the state.

"Lower energy bills, more jobs and higher growth," he continued.

"No more German energy and industrial suicide," he added, responding to response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel calling for political change in the state.

Moscow has in the past offered to resume supplying Germany with cheap gas through the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea if sanctions over its  invasion of Ukraine are lifted.

The AfD has argued that cheaper Russian energy would benefit the German economy and has called for Russian gas supplies to Germany to resume.

However, critics say that Germany's previous reliance on Russian gas made it prone to energy blackmail from Moscow, while buying it would also serve to fuel Moscow's war machine.

Sunday's state election will have no direct bearing on the issue, with Russian pipeline gas subject to European Union sanctions.

Only one of the original four Nord Stream pipeline strands remains intact following explosions that damaged Nord Stream 1 and 2 in 2022. The remaining strand is not in use.

Skip next section Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg

Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg

Crowds rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened on Saturday.

Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.

Beer could not be served until the official opening ceremony at midday, when new Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the environmentalist Greens tapped the first keg with the traditional cry of "O'zapft is" — Bavarian dialect for "It is tapped."

"Hop" over to our story for more about the opening of Oktoberfest.

Skip next section Driver seriously injured in collision with plane at Munich Airport

Driver seriously injured in collision with plane at Munich Airport

The driver of a car operated by a cleaning company has suffered serious injuries in a collision with a plane engine at Munich airport overnight and has been flown to hospital by rescue helicopter, police said Saturday.

The car struck both the engine and then a passenger staircase, a police spokeswoman said, saying that the driver might have been affected by a medical problem before the crash.

The accident, which occurred at around 3. a.m. local time (0100 GMT), is being analyzed to determine the exact cause.

There was never any danger to other people, police said, and flight operations were unaffected.

No scheduled flights are permitted at Munich Airport between midnight and 5 a.m.

Skip next section Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee

Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee

Germany's highest-ranking soldier, General Carsten Breuer, is standing as candidate for the post of chair of the NATO Military Committee at a vote to take place on Saturday in Copenhagen.

The post is currently held by Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone of Italy.

Breuer, 61, will contend against General Marie Annabelle Jennie Carignan, who is currently Chief of the Defence Staff in Canada.

Breuer himself is the current inspector general of the Bundeswehr, or German armed forces.

The winner of the vote would take over leadership of the NATO Military Committee from July 2027.

The head of the committee is seen as the most influential person in NATO alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (Saceur), a position currently held by General Alexus G. Grynkewich of the US Air Force.

entries.title: Decolonizing perceptions about Africa
entries.summary: A UN resolution to redraw the global map to project the African continent more accurately, national initiatives to decolonize schools and a campaign to present positive developments are changing the way Africa is seen.
entries.content:
Africa

Decolonizing perceptions about Africa

September 20, 2026

A UN resolution to redraw the global map to project the African continent more accurately, national initiatives to decolonize schools and a campaign to present positive developments are changing the way Africa is seen.

The Correct the Map resolution to promote map projections that more realistically reflect the true size of continents endorsed by the United Nations in New York at the beginning of September was a huge success for the African countries that led the campaign. In the General Assembly, 164 member states voted to encourage the use of Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps instead of the 16th-century Mercator projection.

Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, which sponsored the Correct the Map campaign at the UN, spoke of a "feeling of pride."

Correct the Map is also supported by the African Union.

"Finally, Africa is fighting to regain its place in the community of nations," he told DW. "The place it has been reserved to this day is unfair. It does not correspond to Africa's reality, not in historical, geographical or economic terms."

Dussey made clear that the debate about global maps was also clearly about symbolically redrawing the maps of facts and knowledge, culture and identity and redressing misperceptions about political and economic realities and power.

Trump's US only state to reject UN resolution

The only UN member state that rejected the resolution was the United States, whose president Donald Trump has engaged in various acts of political symbolism, having issued orders for places to be renamed on maps which he would presumaby also like to redraw Trump has signed executive orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, and Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The UN resolution, meanwhile, is part of a broader, global trend, as French historian Romain Tiquet from the African Worlds Institute (IMAF) told DW.

"Since the late 2000s and early 2010s, there has been a great deal of debate about the decolonization of knowledge — in universities, museums and cultural institutions, as well as within social movements and civil society."

He said many questions were being explored: "Who established the categories through which we conceptualize the world? From which locations? And what power dynamics result from this? And cartography fits right into this context."

Mali breaks with former colonial power France

Many African states have also been trying to free the school systems from colonial influence, often for political reasons.

In October 2025, the Malian government decided to remove French history from the school curriculum. The decision was made to stop teaching about the French Revolution but to focus on Malian history and the other ancient West African kingdoms.

In just a few years, the country's military government has made a clean break with the former colonial power. Mali ended its military cooperation with France in 2022, and French soldiers began to withdraw from the country. Burkina Faso and Niger did the same and the three formed the Alliance of Sahel States in 2023.

Philemon Mtoi from Tumaini University Makumira in Tanzania said Mali had made an important step: "As a historian, I believe that a country without a strong understanding of its own history is like a country without clear leadership and direction. This decision is important because it seeks to strengthen patriotism and foster a stronger sense of national identity."

By investing in the research and preservation of African history, Mali — like Africa as a whole — was making a strong contribution to global scholarship, Mtoi explained.

He spoke of "reclaiming and documenting African histories from an African perspective" and said that this was not only "an act of decolonization" but also an "important step toward intellectual independence."

Mtoi said that many other African countries, such as Ghana, Namibia, South Africa and Kenya, had adopted a similar approach. He added that his own country, Tanzania, had also made major changes to the school curriculum recently. He said that "Tanzanian history and ethics" was now a compulsory subject that had replaced global history and that it would be taught in Swahili, the country's national language.

The historian warned, however, that knowledge of other countries and histories should not be erased. He said it was important to acquire a profound knowledge of significant events in global history, such as the French Revolution, but that this could be done at a later stage.

#NotWaiting campaign to abolish stereotypes

School education in a formal setting is only one part of the puzzle. The non-profit Africa No Filter was one of the organizations behind the Correct the Map campaign. It works to challenge and change harmful narratives about Africa.

In a report titled "The cost of media stereotypes to Africa," it says that "Africa could be losing up to $4.2 billion (€3.6 billion) annually in inflated interest payments due to biased media coverage."

Francois Bouda, an officer for arts and culture at Africa No Filter, said that media outlets continued to portray Africa as being poor, corrupt and crisis-ridden. The new campaign #NotWaiting is meant to change this perception.

"We are addressing Africans because we, too, need to change the way we view the African continent. We've accepted the image of a continent incapable of taking care of itself, one that is poor and has no opportunities. We've internalized this and come to believe it, even though many positive things are happening. First of all there has to be an internal change," said Bouda.

'Millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day'

The #NotWaiting campaign is part of a larger movement, which aims to highlight positive developments and initiatives in Africa, to focus on political programs and actors, to counter crisis-reporting.

It comprises figures on the continent and in the diaspora, people who are "not waiting for an external hand to dictate what path to follow," said Bouda.

"This is good for Africans," he said, adding that there were many actors but that the only problem was that they "aren't visible."

The campaign is about Africans themselves painting a positive picture of Africa as a continent on the move, about people sharing stories, which are not curated by international institutions or media outlets.

"We've been building all along," says a video clip to promote the campaign. "From village roads to crowded cities, across the 54 countries that make up the continent, millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day."

This article, to which Sandrine Blanchard and Jean-Claude Abalo contributed, was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany: Polls open in two key state elections
entries.summary: Voting in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is expected to bring gains for the far-right AfD party and could determine whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz can hold on to power. Follow DW live.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Polls open in two key state elections

Published September 20, 2026last updated September 20, 2026

Voting in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is expected to bring gains for the far-right AfD party and could determine whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz can hold on to power. Follow DW live.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Regional elections are taking place in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state Berlin
  • Voters are also electing members of district assemblies in Berlin
  • The outcome of the elections could determine the political future of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose approval rating is at a record low
  • The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to gain ground in both states but is unlikely to be part of government
  • For the first time, 16- and 17-year-olds are eligible to vote in both states

We're expecting exit polls at around 16.00 GMT. Follow along here for all the highs and lows today:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Candidates cast votes in key state elections

Candidates cast votes in key state elections

Voters have been lining up at polling stations to cast their ballots, as have the candidates (presumably to vote for themselves) in Berlin and in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

In the German capital, Werner Graf (Green Party) and Steffen Krach (center-left Social Democrats) cast their votes in the Tempelhof-Schöneberg constituency.

Further north, Leif-Erik Holm (far-right AfD) cast his vote in Schwerin, the capital of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Holm told local public broadcaster NDR outside the polling station that he was "optimistic" about his party's chances.

"The clouds have parted and the sky is turning blue," he said, referring to the color of his party.

His rival, the incumbent state premier Manuela Schwesig (Social Democrats), cast her vote a short time later.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners

IN DEPTH: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners

A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.

Find out more about how foreigners are not included in Berlin's elections in this report.

Skip next section WATCH: Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor?

WATCH: Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor?

In the run-up to Berlin's election, Elif Eralp's socialist Left Party is narrowly ahead in major polls — setting up a close race with the conservative CDU. But her party faces controversy over antisemitic rhetoric.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?

IN DEPTH: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?

Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck.

Here's a look at key economic issues that could influence the election.

Skip next section WATCH: German local election races taking place after AfD's historic victory in Saxony Anhalt

WATCH: German local election races taking place after AfD's historic victory in Saxony Anhalt

The elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are taking place two weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged to first place in Saxony-Anhalt, securing nearly 44% of the vote in the state.

Here's what you need to know:

Skip next section WATCH: Is Berlin heading for its Mamdani moment?

WATCH: Is Berlin heading for its Mamdani moment?

The Left Party is hoping to secure its candidate Elif Eralp as mayor of the capital city if the party finishes in the first place in state elections. Here's what you need to know about her:

Skip next section Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election guide: What you need to know

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election guide: What you need to know

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the fight is between the Social Democrats (SPD) led by the popular Manuela Schwesig and the far-right Altnerative for Germany (AfD).

The 52-year-old Schwesig has made it her mission to beat back the advance of the AfD, which is polling at around 37%, ahead of the SPD at 33%.

"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW recently. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."

What to watch out for in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Besides keeping tabs on whether the AfD comes out on top, all eyes are also on how the CDU performs in the state.

CDU is the conservative Christian Democratic Union party that is chaired by the chancellor of the country, Friedrich Merz.

His party is polling at around 7% in the state, which is slightly above the 5% threshold required by a party to enter state parliament.

In the 2021 elections, the CDU had just 13.3% of the vote.

If the CDU fails to achieve the 5% threshold, there's going to be immense pressure on Merz to fight for his job.

Who are the main candidates?

SPD: Manuela Schwesig, also the incumbent state premier.

AfD: Leif-Erik Holm is the AfD's candidate for state premier, whom the party would put forward to head the state government if it can form one, while Enrico Schult is the AfD's candidate leading the party's election campaign in the state. Holm is the better-known candidate out of the two.

CDU: Daniel Peters, who has been the chair of the CDU parliamentary group in the state parliament.

The Left (Die Linke): Simon Oldenburg, who is the current minister for education in the state.

What's the likeliest scenario?

Even if the AfD comes out on top in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, that's not a guarantee that it will govern the state.

In Germany's parliamentary system, a party needs a majority in the state parliament or coalition partners to elect a state premier.

That means that the AfD could be pushed to the sidelines if other parties reject cooperation with it under the so-called "firewall" policy. 

Skip next section Berlin election guide: What you need to know

Berlin election guide: What you need to know

The campaign so far has been dominated by a battle between the far-left Left Party and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)

Both parties are neck and neck, according to polling in recent weeks.

If Merz's party wins the elections, that'll be good news for the chancellor, whose popularity has taken a big hit, especially following state elections in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounced the CDU.

Seventeen parties are contesting the election in Berlin, including the Left Party and the CDU. The four other major parties are the AfD — which has consistently polled in third place —, the environmentalist Green Party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the left-wing, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

What is the top issue for Berlin voters?

With the German capital struggling with a severe housing shortage in a city where 85% rent their homes, housing and rental costs are voters' top concerns.

Advertised rents have doubled since 2014, and the city needs 211,000 more homes by 2040.

So far, the Left Party has been the only major party that has promised to act on a 2021 referendum when 59% of Berliners voted to have the government take control of apartments from the biggest landlords to protect rents.

For the AfD, Berlin's housing crisis has fed into its argument for restricting immigration that has driven support for the party.

Who are the main candidates?

  • CDU: Stefan Evers is the CDU's lead candidate after the outgoing mayor, Kai Wegner, withdrew from the race.
  • The Left Party (Die Linke): Elif Eralp will be leading her party into an election as its lead candidate for the first time. She was born in Munich to Turkish parents. She has been compared to Zohran Mamdani, the democratic socialist who won the New York City mayor race following his campaign around an affordability agenda for residents of his city.
  • The Greens (Die Grünen): The Greens are fielding a two-person team consisting of Bettina Jarasch and Werner Graf.
  • AfD (Alternative for Germany): Kristin Brinker has campaigned on issues of crime and immigration.
  • SPD: Steffen Krach, who has experience working in the Berlin city government and was until recently a top politician in Hanover, the capital of Lower Saxony.

Skip next section Germany's state elections and the fate of Chancellor Merz: What to know

Germany's state elections and the fate of Chancellor Merz: What to know

Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a rare campaign appearance for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at an event in Berlin on Thursday but has largely stayed away from the campaign trail.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU might even fail to make the 5% threshold required to enter parliament.

At the national level, Merz's own approval ratings fell to as low as 14% earlier in the week , while the far-right AfD has surged to first place with 27-29%, according to opinion polls released earlier this week.

Merz's CDU was polling nationally at 18-20%.

The chancellor has been under mounting pressure over whether he's the right person for the job, amid frustration over the slow pace of his promised reforms and the rise of the AfD.

Merz insisted this week that he's still committed to leading the nation and his governing coalition with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

"I was elected for four years and I want to use this time to solve problems," he said on Tuesday, insisting: "We have to prove that this ​can be achieved with ‌this coalition."

However, a YouGov survey released on Friday showed that around half of Germans don't expect Merz to still be chancellor by the end of the year. 

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen and welcome to our coverage of elections in Berlin and the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Polling stations are open for voters to elect members of the state parliaments. There's also a third vote open to EU citizens for electing members of one of Berlin's 12 district or borough assemblies.

While the elections are regional, they are set to have a national impact, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose popularity has severely dipped in recent weeks, struggling to keep his job.

That's due to a host of reasons, including the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) that secured a historic result with nearly 44% of the vote in elections two weeks ago in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

In Berlin, the race is tied between the Christian Democratic Party (CDU) and the Left Party (Die Linke). The AfD has consistently been polling third in Berlin, which is both the capital city and one of the country's 16 states.

In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the race is tied between the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the AfD.

Stay tuned for the latest developments in these two crucial elections throughout the day.

entries.title: Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
entries.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's record-low approval ratings have emboldened his opponents. There are three ways to remove a chancellor from office in Germany.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?

September 20, 2026

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's record-low approval ratings have emboldened his opponents. There are three ways to remove a chancellor from office in Germany.

It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners,  Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?

Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.

In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election. 

The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.

But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.

Option 1: Resignation

Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.

Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved the necessary majority, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.

How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.

Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence

If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.

An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.

The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no-confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.

Option 3: A confidence vote

Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.

As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.

Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.

If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.

It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.

So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Dutch police disperse violent far-right protest in The Hague
entries.summary: After violence broke out, Dutch riot police dispersed hundreds of far-right protesters in The Hague. Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.
entries.content:
Netherlands

Dutch police disperse violent far-right protest in The Hague

September 20, 2026

After violence broke out, Dutch riot police dispersed hundreds of far-right protesters in The Hague. Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.

Dutch riot police on Saturday clashed with approximately 500 far-right protesters who chanted antisemitic slogans at a rally in The Hague city center.

The protesters threw fireworks and other projectiles at the police.

According to AFP reporters on the scene, police used baton charges and specialist dogs to break up the demonstration.

What do we know about the protest

The "We Are the People" rally was organized to protest government policies, particularly those related to immigration.

Protesters had planned to march through the city, but local authorities banned the march when violence broke out in the park where protesters were gathering. Authorities then ordered the demonstration to break up.

The police said that they arrested 24 people and used water cannons to disperse the rioters. They added that further investigations are underway.

How did the authorities react

On X, Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had deliberately sought confrontation with the police and had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.

Meanwhile, Justice Minister David van Weel called for an "extremely firm" response to the "disgusting scenes" that occurred at the protest.

Van Weel said demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, attacked police, and threw fireworks at riot officers.

Saturday's unrest occurred one year after riots broke out during a right-wing demonstration.

During clashes between black-clad protesters and police, a police car was set on fire, and the headquarters of the centrist D66 party — whose leader, Rob Jetten, is now prime minister — was attacked.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
entries.summary: The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.

The summer (June to August) of 2026 was the warmest in Europe since records began, beating the record set in 2003, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service,

Not only that, Germany's DWD weather service says that there was an "unprecedented" number of hot days this year. "On average across Germany,there were about 22 hot days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees Celsius and about five very hot days with temperatures of at least 35 degrees Celsius," the DWD wrote in in a press release at the end of August.

The estimated number of heat-related deaths also reached unprecedented levels, with at least 16,300 people dying by the end of August, even if few of them died directly because of the heat, but rather as a consequence of underlying health conditions exacerbated by the heat.

The figures were compiled from a statistical correlation between the number of deaths recorded by Germany's Federal Statistical Office and the temperatures measured by the DWD during a specific period.

Heat-related deaths in Germany are more likely if the average weekly temperature reaches 20 degrees Celsius or more. This is the average of all hourly temperatures recorded in a week, including at nighttime.

This year, the average weekly temperatures in the country rose above the 20-degree mark several times. It was particularly hot at the end of June, when the average weekly temperature reached above 26 degrees between the 22nd and 28th of the month.

Excess mortality during heat waves

Though it is not possible to determine a cause of death using statistics, researchers and medical professionals have a good understanding of how heat affects the human body, and there is widespread consensus that excess mortality during heat waves is possible.

"It was not just the high temperatures on the thermometer that were important, but also how long the heat lasted and the fact that it hardly cooled down at night," said Andreas Matzarakis, professor of environmental meteorology at Freiburg University.

Many people have trouble sleeping on hot nights. Yet, getting enough sleep is important so that the body can recover from the heat and stress of the day.

Matzarakis said that the severity of heat stress was not related solely to air temperatures. Humidity, solar radiation and wind also played a role — and what is known as the 'felt' temperature. He said that humidity and still air could place a heavy strain on the body, even in moderate temperatures.

Underprivileged most vulnerable

The less privileged members of society were also among the most vulnerable, said Martin Röösli, environmental scientist at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Basel. "They are more likely to live in homes that are not well insulated or are more likely to work outdoors."

A large proportion of those who died because of the heat probably had only a short life expectancy left, due to their age and medical conditions, but Röösli said that there was a consensus that "some of the deceased could have lived for a long time and were simply in a fragile state at the time of the heat wave."

For Alexandra Schneider, a meteorologist and epidemiologist at the Helmholtz center in Munich in southern Germany, the deaths that occurred during the heat waves were very likely not only because of the "harvesting effect," which describes "how a heat wave causes very vulnerable individuals in particular to die a few days or weeks prematurely."

Had this been the case, there would have been a deficit of mortality in the following weeks, which did not happen. Thus, she believes, a significant proportion of those who died could have lived on for months or even years.

This article was translated from German.
